_note: PRINTED-OPTION DEFECT: TWO of the four alternatives are 'not correct' as printed, so the question as set has two answers. Option (C) is false and is plainly the intended answer - the chapter's own characteristic (1) of the vector product prints \(\vec{P} \times \vec{Q} \ne \vec{Q} \times \vec{P}\) as Eq. (2.20). Option (D) is ALSO false as printed, because its second term reads \(\vec{B} \times \vec{C}\) where the distributive law requires \(\vec{A} \times \vec{C}\); the chapter prints that law correctly as Eq. (2.21), \(\vec{A} \times (\vec{B} + \vec{C}) = \vec{A} \times \vec{B} + \vec{A} \times \vec{C}\). Verified on the rendered page at 6x - option (D) unambiguously reads \(\vec{B} \times \vec{C}\). So (D) is a typographical corruption of a statement the book itself prints correctly, and the key is retained on (C). Candidate for an errata bracket (NOT applied in this pass).
solution: [Textbook misprint in a distractor: one alternative is printed as \(\vec{A} \times (\vec{B} + \vec{C}) = \vec{A} \times \vec{B} + \vec{B} \times \vec{C}\), where the second term should read \(\vec{A} \times \vec{C}\). Taken literally that statement is also incorrect, so as printed the question has two answers. The keyed answer is nevertheless the intended one and is not in doubt: the option set is built as three true identities and one false, the false one being that the cross product commutes, and this chapter prints the distributive law correctly at Eq. (2.21) with \(\vec{A} \times \vec{C}\). The stem is preserved as printed rather than repaired, so a reader who spots the typo can see it.]
